name: Acorn
challenge_context: Welcome to the Acorn Neighborhood. You are currently standing outside of the Oakland Unified School district headquarters. Specifically, you are standing at the part of the property that used to be the location of the Cole Grammar School. Jack London attended this school from 1887-1891 and it later burned down in 1923. In 1901 it caught some attention from the San Francisco Call for the following story titled "Pet Rat Poisons Nature Study." The story was written as follows: "An untoward accident broke up the class in nature study yesterday in Miss Robina Ferguson's room in the Cole Grammar School. Miss Bertha Chapman, who supervises the department of nature study, instructed the pupils a day or two ago that they should each fetch a household pet to school on Friday in order to make studies of their peculiarities. When Miss Chapman called the class to attention in the afternoon she found her request had been taken literally. There were sufficient animals on hand to stock a Barnum annex. In the midst of the studying something happened to start the girls to the high places and the boys upon a hot pursuit. By some unaccountable means a white rat that belongs to one of the boys got out of its cage. It was detected by a brindle cat, which gave it a run for life. The proprietor of the white rat pursued the cat in an attempt to rescue the rodent. Stirred to fever heat by the excitement, a big Newfoundland dog joined in the race. Soon every boy in the room was doing his best to herd the rat into a corner. Teachers and girl pupils sought safety on the chairs. Not until the cat caught the rat was order restored."
challenge: The Challenge: You will text me for a list of 10 animals and then upon receipt set a 2 minute timer and order the animals from biggest to smallest (on average). Text me back and I will tell you how many you got correct. Anything above 7 correct wins you the challenge. If you get fewer than 7, wait 5 minutes and try again.

challenge_context:

It is also known that it was the home of Butch's Record Mill for some time in the 1960s. Attached is an advertisment for this. Because of this we will be looking at some Oakland records.

name: Chinatown
challenge_context: Welcome to Chinatown. Chinatown is one of Oakland's oldest neighborhoods and one of the oldest Chinatowns in the US, from its beginning in 1850. You are at Lincoln Square Park, one of a few public parks in Chinatown. This park features a playstructure in the shape of a boat. Specifically, in the shape of a junk boat. Click here for a picture of the placard which explains this history. The English word "junk" is supposedly derived from the name of these boats. The Portuguse called these boats junco, and that came from the Malay word jong, which came from the Javanese djong. The Chinese had chuán boats, which were then all called junk boats.
challenge: The Challenge: Go to a nearby store and buy one item of Chinese "junk food" and have everyone try it. That's it, the only way to fail is to not do this. Text me a picture of you all with the food and you've won the neighborhood.

name: Downtown
challenge_context: Welcome to Downtown Oakland! You are standing in the area that in 1853 housed the Contra Costa Academy, opened by Rev. Henry Durant. In 1855 it became the College of California. Then after calls for a State University in 1867, Gov. Henry Haight sign an act that established the University of California. This made the College of California into the College of Letter, and then the year after it became a university. It stayed down here in Oakland until 1873, when the Berkeley campus opened with its 3rd president, Daniel Gilman. of College Hall at its 12th and Harrison location. Now comes the part of the story that doesn't include men who became street names. About 109 years after the opening of the first building a group of students took a cigar box and started a student run radio station they called Radio KAL. In 1967, it officially became KALX. Since then it has survived Governor Reagan issued lockdowns during protests against troops on the ground in Cambodia during the Vietnam War. Had students interview Charles Manson. And much more found here. As a part of that history Someone pulled a highlight list of songs that were played at KALX between 1970 and 1977. Firesign Theatre – I Think We’re All Bozos on This Bus (1971) Dick Gregory at Kent State (1971) Sweathog – Sweathog (1972) Emerson, Lake, and Palmer – Pictures at an Exhibition (1972) Monty Python – Matching Tie & Handkerchief (1975) Disco Tex and His Sex-o-Lettes (1975) Chuck Mangione – Bellavia (1975) Jimmy Buffett – Havana Daydream (1976) Lou Reed – Coney Island Baby (1976) Peter Frampton – Frampton Comes Alive (1976) Today, the show at KALX that is playing should be "Sunspot" or "I Scream Sundaze Tumble Weed". Stream it here as you read the challenge.

Call KALX at 510-642-5259 and request any of the songs from the above playlist. Or, also, you can just request a song you want to hear or seems on theme with whatever the DJ is playing.

name: Harmon/Lorin
challenge_context: Welcome to the Harmon-Lorin neighborhood. In the early 20th century this neighborhood had a lot of Japanese immigrants, who were shamefully forcibly removed during WWII. After WWII, this neighborhood saw a lot of migration of Black southerners. In the 1960s during the building of the BART system, there was the possibility of putting elevated rail in the neighborhood as was done in other areas. It was not until a community activist, Mable Howard, a 63 year old black woman, filed a lawsuit which forced the BART line and its accompanying station to go underground. In her words she did not want a Berlin Wall in Berkeley, as it would have divided and degraded the neighborhood. The sculpture you are in front of was made by Mable's daughter and artist, Mildred Howard.  The sculpture is inspired by the traditional West African metal work that existed as both currency and jewelry. The currency aspect is important, as it pays tribute to the wealth that was created by the African Americans in the region and what Mable sought to keep intact.
challenge: The Challenge: Text me when you are ready and I will reply with a list of 10 West African countries and a list of 10 currencies. You will have to match the country to the currency. You can do this with a piece of paper and then text me your answers. You have 5 minutes to do this. You will need to get at least 6/10 correct to win the neighborhood. If you get them incorrect wait 5 minutes and try again. Good luck!

name: Harrison St - Oakland Ave
challenge_context: Hello welcome to the Harrison St/Oakland Ave neighborhood. Probably one of the worst named neighborhoods. You are standing in front of a Whole Foods. That Whole Foods building used to be the a powerhouse and central depot for the Key System. And to the right of that was Piedmont Baths . An imposing brick structure comprising a natatorium with galleries, dressing rooms, hot tubs, massage areas, and a café, it was built to promote interest in the appeal of East Bay living for pre-earthquake citizens of SF who did not have a similar facility at the time. Until 1904, the baths used waste steam heat from the Key System powerhouse to heat the swimming tank. They pumped water from the Lake and Estuary to fill the pools, and had a complex gravity-based filter to ensure the safety of the water, in one of the first implementations of charcoal, sand, and gravel filters of the Hyatt Patent. The baths were open until 1927, when a fire damaged the facility. Unfortunately, during the lifespan of the baths, multiple people died mysteriously at the baths.
challenge: The Challenge: Make cucumber water! Go into Whole Foods and get the ingredients for a cucumber water. If you have any moral qualms with Amazon/Whole Foods, feel free to walk to the nearby Sprouts/Grocery Outlet and complete the challenge. Text me a picture of your cucumber water and you win the neighborhood!

name: Jack London Square
challenge_context:
Welcome to Jack London Square. A lovely waterfront neighborhood that houses the main Oakland Ferry terminal, the Amtrak terminal, and a weekly farmer's market. 
This is named after the famous writer Jack London, who grew up in Oakland and spent a lot of his time in the area as a kid. 
Technically the square only refers to the area south of Embarcadero West, the street the train tracks are on. Now the name refers to the whole area below 880. 
That other part of the neighborhood has also been referred to as Produce and Waterfront due to the large outdoor produce markets that once stood there, although there is still plenty of produce in the warehouses in the area. 
In 1905, to get away from San Francisco after having achieved success with the printing of his first book, the Sea-Wolf, London bought some land in Glen Ellen in Sonoma County. After his death, his wife inherited the property and after her death the state of California inherited it. This became Jack London State Historic Park. 
The park has orchards that consists of apple, pear, apricot, peach, cherry, and plum trees that were planted between 1908-1912. In 2012, efforts were started to stabilize this and in recent years nearly 800 lbs of fruit from the area were gathered and donated to those experiencing food insecurity.
challenge: The Challenge: There is a farmer's market today in Jack London. Go to the farmer's market and buy one of the fruits listed above that were found in Jack London's orchards and sit at one of the benches facing the water and enjoy the fruit. You just need to buy one piece of fruit and take a picture of it with the water in the background. Text me the picture and you win the neighborhood.

challenge_context:
Welcome to the Lakeside neighborhood! You are in front of the Lake Chalet. This building was originally built in 1909 as a salt water pumping station for the Oakland Fire Dept to get water from Lake Merritt in case of very serious fires like the ones that were seen after the 1906 earthquake.  
Lake Merritt was designated the first wildlife refuge in the US in 1870 and is home to at least 140 different types of birds.
challenge: The Challenge: This website has 72 of those 140 bird species. Your task is to find and take pictures of as many of these bird species as you can. When you're done, text me the number of bird species that you found and I will give you your next task.

name: Longfellow
challenge_context: Welcome to Longfellow! A neighborhood named after the poet and his eponymous elementary school in the neighborhood. David Hilliard and Huey Newton, the Black Panthers, had their childhood homes here and the second Black Panther Party offices were housed in this neighborhood. Nancy Reagan visited the elementary school as a part of a War on Drugs tour and allegedly coined the phrase "Just Say No" here. You are standing in front of Marcus Books, a bookstore founded by Drs. Raye & Julian Richardson, who met at Tuskegee University. Julian started Success Printing Co. in 1946 in the Fillmore and in 1960 they both founded Marcus Books (named after Marcus Garvey). Marcus Books boasts itself as the oldest Black-owned independent bookstore in the United States. They have hosted a number of authors, such as: Toni Morrison, Rosa Parks, Muhammad Ali, Maya Angelou, Walter Mosley, Angela Davis, Terry McMillan, Chaka Khan, Michael Eric Dyson, Iyanla Vanzant, Sister Souljah, Nikki Giovanni, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, and Patti LaBelle.

name: Mosswood
challenge_context: Welcome to Mosswood. Specifically to the mansion at Mosswood Park. This house is the namesake of this park, as it was the home and estate of J. Mora Moss and Julia Wood (Moss). After they both passed without having had any children, the citizens of Oakland asked the city to buy the land and turn it into a park. After renaming various streets to form MacArthur Boulevard, 8 1/2-year-old Franklyn Delano Winston had the idea to also rename Mosswood Park in honor of General MacArthur, and the suggestion was quickly adopted and a new sign put up. But H.F. Deaner, age 91, and others protested the name change before the city council because of the history of the Mosswood name, and barely a month later the decision was made to change it back to Mosswood Park.

name: Oak Center
challenge_context: Welcome to Oak Center. You're in DeFremery Park or Lil Bobby Hutton Park. Like Mosswood Park, there is an old Victorian in the middle of the park. It has seen many things, like one of two Oakland stops in JFK's 1960 election tour. It was a key location for many Black Panther rallies, and activities like the distribution of free groceries. As far as I can tell from my own research in Oakland newspapers, it was likely the location of the first Juneteenth celebration in Oakland in 1967. It also has seen stranger more unique activities that I have only found one or two newspaper stories of. Such as: - In 1908, Isabella J Martin, a career criminal, scammer, and murderer was under suspicion of trying to kill Oakland Judge Ogden was snitched on by her son "Baby John" Martin, who showed Oakland police where he had hidden explosives and poison at the Park under his mom's instruction. Specifically, the police found "forty sticks of dynamite, a quart bottle of muriatic acid, and a quantity of fuses and screw-eyes." Baby John said "this is the store from which she expected to draw her materials for bombs with which to exterminate her enemies." - In 1909, two men took white sand from the park and bagged it and passed it off to housewives as sugar. They were eventually arrested for their trickery. -A gunman locked two of the police station's attendants in the restroom, then emptied a cash register of $309 and ran off. He was spotted by a police officer who chased him for two blocks and the two exchanged half a dozen shots. The exchange ended when the officer ran into a tree and knocked himself unconscious. The thief got away and the officer was found after neighbors called police who found the first officer at the foot of a tree in the park.

name: Old Oakland
challenge_context: Welcome to Old Oakland, specifically to Lafayette Square Park. In the 1880s Oakland Public Schools Superintendent Jewett Gilson, got the idea to build an observatory here, but he needed the money. Anthony Chabot decided to offer up the money to do so, with the stipulation that the telescope be available for public use at no cost. The observatory was built in 1883, but in 1915 due to light pollution it was moved into the hills, and then once more in 1975 to its current location. However, despite those moves, the telescope used at the Observatory is still the same one that Anthony Chabot donated in 1883. It is still free for public viewing, although for only 6 hours during the whole week.

It was first mentioned in January 1922 because 28 bottles of some alcoholic concoction was found and then turned over to the feds to determine how much alcohol it had. In July of that same year, they were arrested after a raid found 12 barrels containing 750 gallons of wine in their possession.
They ended up almost beating these charges in April 1923 after their lawyer successfully argued that the wine appeared there after the sun had randomly fermented some grape juice in their possession. I am not sure how this was successfully argued, as they had already plead guilty and were fined $10. Presumably this business closed around this time as that same month their soft drink license had been removed.

name: Shafter
challenge_context:
Welcome to the Shafter neighborhood. If this were Chicago, it would be called Lower Lower Rockridge. It's almost Temescal, but not really. However, it does have a part of Temescal in it. 
The Temescal creek runs from Lake Temescal in Upper Rockridge all the way to Emeryville, but the section of it here was culverted in the 70s and 80s, meaning the true stream of the creek went underground. 
You can still see where it would have cut through in Shafter, because of the Rockridge-Temescal Greenbelt (interesting they left out the Shafter name). 
Today, walking in this Greenbelt, you can still see remnants of the creek through public art and the faux reconstituted creek that sometimes runs through it.

Take a picture of the boat going down the creek and send it to me to win the Shafter neighborhood. Don't forget to give it a name on the side of the boat. Also, if you haven't done the Lower Rockridge, or Fairview Park challenges, I definitely recommend walking up the Greenway. The Farmer's Market is also going to be there, good place to grab a snack. Ok one last thing. I hardly know her.

name: Temescal
challenge_context:
Welcome to Temescal. This is probably the first challenge that you see in this game, so welcome to the game! Temescal is one of the oldest neighborhoods in Oakland, but before it was a neighborhood it was actually its own town. Before that, it was an unincorporated village built up on the estate of Vincente Peralta. Before that it was an area partially inhabited by the Chochenyo-speaking people, an ethnic subset of the Ohlone people. The name Temescal is an interesting one because it is technically an indigenous name, just not indigenous to here. Temescalli means sweat lodge in Nahuatl, and the story goes that the Spanish colonizers named this area that since they saw similar sweat lodges built along Temescal creek. 
In 1896 the northernmost boundary of Oakland was 36th street, and in 1897 the citizens of Temescal voted to join Oakland to benefit from the school and police systems of the town. 
Between 1910 and 1930, Temescal had one of the largest Italian populations in California. And Temescal was largely Italian up until the 1960s. As the children of the families that had lived there for decades started to grow older and move to the suburbs and the older people that owned the homes died, and those houses that had been in the families for years started to become available to other non-Italian families. This is a nicer telling of the story; Sewall Glinternick tells a different one: he basically recounts how a realtor, usually a Black realtor, would offer a white homeowner that wanted to leave more money than their house was worth and that homeowner would have no choice but to sell and he'd help a Black family move in. Once that family moved in the rest of the block would panic, get desparate, and start trying to leave the neighborhood. And as homes sold more and more families would "panic." This was called block busting. 
Shortly thereafter Temescal became a primarily Black, working class neighborhood. In recent decades, another shift has happened as the neighborhood has gentrified. 
Some other fun facts about Temescal:
- The former Walgreens on 51st and Telegraph used to be a horse barn for the horse street cars that led to Berkeley, and then became a car barn when a mechanized street car was put in. 
- The current Whole Foods used to be a park called Humboldt Park, as Telegraph used to be called Humboldt. It also used to be a theatre called the Claremont theatre, which spent its final days as a adult theatre known as the Pussycat Theatre. 
Okay... why did I tell you all of this information about Temescal? Read the challenge below. Honestly, hopefully you skipped this and just went to the challenge and are now reading this part to complete the challenge.
challenge: The Challenge: Go to the East Bay Creative Reuse depot and each team member should find an old postcard from somewhere they have been. Then write a postcard to a friend or family member and tell them something that you've just learned about Temescal. Keep the cards on you and I'll find you during the day to give you a postage stamp and you can drop them in a blue box. Text me a picture of you all with the postcards and you'll win the neighborhood.

name: Uptown
challenge_context:
Welcome to Uptown or is it welcome Up-town? Anyway, most people think this neighborhood name is a recent rebranding to assist gentrification. However, that name has been in use for nearly two centuries. 
In the 1853, the map of Oakland ended at 14th street. And as Oakland grew to the north, the area above that line became "Up-Town." The first mention of this is in 1895, in a mention of the Tribune opening an office space Up-Town. From then on, you can regularly find advertisements and articles that mention the Uptown district. In fact, you can find walking tours from the 1980s that highlight the historic Uptown District.
challenge: The Challenge: Do a walking tour! Use this printed out and marked up Art Deco terra cotta walking tour from 1985. The tour has each destination highlighted in yellow, blue, and pink. You will need to visit at least 2 buildings from each color and pass around the map so you can tell each other about the buildings. Text me which buildings you visited and you win this neighborhood.
